catalog_quote: Kugama has stem-initial prominence.10 Prosodic prominence implies the presence of one prominent syllable per phonological word.11 Thus, in Kugama the first syllable of the stem is strong whereas the following syllables of the stem are prosodically weak. I mainly focus on phonological evidence for stem-initial prosodic prominence in Kugama. I have not analyzed differences between prosodically strong and weak positions in terms of intensity and duration. In Table 16, I provide some features of prosodically strong and weak positions. ... [fn. 11] I use the term phonological word to refer to the combination of a stem and following enclitics. ... [p. 46] Stem-initial position is a prosodically strong position in which the following syllables can occur: V, CV, VV, CVV, VC, and CVC. Prosodically weak position is restricted to the CV syllable type. ... [p. 47] All three tone levels are found in prosodically strong and weak positions. ... Contour tones, which are sequences of different level tones, commonly occur in prosodically strong position. ... [2.6.1] The Kugama tone system consists of three contrastive level tones: High (H), Mid (M), and Low (L).

new_statements.rule_in_words: Kugama is a three-tone language (H, M, L) with stem-initial prosodic prominence of the Niger-Congo type: the first syllable of the stem is the single prominent syllable of the phonological word (stem + enclitics); all following stem syllables and enclitics are weak. Prominence is diagnosed distributionally (full consonant, vowel, syllable-type and contour-tone inventories only in the initial syllable; weak syllables are CV with mostly short front vowels and no contours), not acoustically; the author does not use the term 'stress'.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None mentioned; exactly one prominent syllable per phonological word.
new_statements.exceptions: Ideophones, reduplicated forms, borrowings and historically complex forms may have heavy non-initial syllables (e.g. sīzáā 'children', bìmɛ́ɛ̰̄ 'body'); some functional monosyllables (bound nouns, construct forms, prepositions, pronominals, definite marker =rɛ̂(ʔ)) are ambiguous between prominent and weak status; the definite marker exceptionally carries a contour tone in weak position.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the phonological word defined as stem plus following enclitics (all clitics are enclitics and prosodically weak); prominence is stem-initial, i.e. morphologically anchored, which in this enclitic-only language coincides with word-initial. Statement is phonological/distributional; no phonetic (intensity/duration) analysis and no claim about phrase-level stress.
new_statements.identity_note: The thesis describes Kugama (autonym-based name Wam also used by the author in 2018-2019 talks), ISO kow, Glottolog kuga1239 'Gengle-Kugama'; the HAL keywords list Kuga1239 explicitly. Meek (1931) grouped Gengle with Kugama; the thesis is on Kugama proper (fieldwork with Kugama speakers, Adamawa State), not a separate Gengle variety.

sources.note: Ch. 2 Phonology has a dedicated section 2.3 'Prosodic prominence' (pp. 45-47): Kugama has stem-initial prominence, one prominent syllable per phonological word (stem + enclitics); first stem syllable strong, following syllables and enclitics weak; evidence is distributional (consonant/vowel/syllable-type/contour-tone asymmetries), author explicitly has not measured intensity/duration. Three contrastive level tones H, M, L (section 2.6). The word 'stress' never occurs in the thesis.
